subject: Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)
parts:
Hi,

Forgive my posting a question on here about quite a general estimation problem, but I always find the insight of the Stan community to be far superior than other fora.

I am trying to determine the performance of a yet-to-be-determined estimator of a particular aspect of a distribution, by doing Monte Carlo testing of it over a number of samples from a particular distribution. Because I am looking to evaluate the estimator's properties, I am wanting to repeat the estimation process probably tens of thousands of times. So whatever the estimation process, it needs to be fast.

The snag is that I can't determine the PDF of this distribution (it involves a mixture of a normal with a bespoke survival-type distribution). Nor can I determine the moments of this distribution; they are without-doubt, analytically intractable.

However, I can draw samples from this distribution at a reasonable pace: 100 samples in less than 0.05s, and 1000 samples in 0.15s, for example.

Up until now, I have been working with a surrogate distribution, whose moments are well-characterised, and have been using generalised method of moments to equate the sample moments, with their population equivalents. Note: I don't like method of moments, I am just using it here, because I don't see another equally-fast choice (I would prefer maximum likelihood, or even better, a Bayesian equivalent, but I can't see a way here.)

The surrogate distribution does quite well at emulating the first couple of moments of the true distribution from which I'm sampling. However, the higher moments are nowhere near. This means that the estimator shows some bias, that is undesirable for its application.

I've also tried matching the characteristic functions of the empirical and actual data, but this method is struggling to produce any accuracy at all.

Given the speed of being able to draw samples from the true distribution, I was wondering whether there was an alternative way to go. Essentially something like ABC, but it would have to be faster. This might be possible, because all I want is a point estimate. An alternative would be to construct an empirical likelihood, then maximise this. However, before jumping in, I wanted to tap the estimation-skill of the Stan community.

Does anyone have any ideas?

Best,

Ben

PS If you need details of the surrogate distribution, then look at my question here: http://mathematica.stackexchange.com/questions/108052/estimate-parameters-of-a-derived-distribution - it basically has the shape of a survival distribution, with gaussian noise added. The actual distribution is similar, but with quite different 3rd and higher moments.

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Re: Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)
parts:
An idea which occurs to me, which is to generate a large number of samples from my distribution to each set of parameters. So for each parameter set I have a cluster of samples. I can then calculate properties of those samples: mean, variance, eCDF and so on, for each parameter set. 

Each time I want to estimate parameters, I just look for the cluster whose characteristics are most similar to the data sample at hand. Simple, messy, and I'm sure done before. Essentially this is a bit like maximising an empirical likelihood, or perhaps more closely, a empirical method of moments estimator.

Has anyone come across this type of method before? Alternatively, if you think it's a terrible idea, I'd also like to know!

Best,

Ben

messages.author: ee490f1373633c05
messages.subject: Re: Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)
parts:
Perhaps use some sort of mixture model approximation - eg draw 100 samples, and use an n=100 basis kernel density estimate as an approximation.

This will converge to the actual PDF with a sufficiently large number of samples.  The only question then is what is "sufficiently large" to be useful for you, and how to choose the bandwidth.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)
parts:
If you can draw samples from the distribution then that usually
means your model is intractable due to an intractable integrable.
But HMC is really good at doing that already — so you should
be able to incorporate this by adding more nuisance parameters
and just letting Stan fit the entire joint model.
